title: Glucose-HR coupling rigidity is timescale-selective: strongest at ultradian scales
statement: The diabetes-associated increase in glucose-HR coupling is not uniform across timescales. It is strongest at ultradian frequencies (1-4 hour oscillations corresponding to meal-driven glucose excursions and postprandial autonomic responses), weaker at high-frequency scales (<30 min, dominated by activity artifacts and HR noise), and absent or reversed at circadian scales (>8h, reflecting preserved gross day-night organization). This predicts that wavelet coherence between glucose and HR at 1-4h periods will show a larger diabetes severity gradient (Cohen's d > 0.6) than coherence at <30min or >8h periods.
mechanism: Postprandial glucose excursions trigger sympathetic activation and HR acceleration through hepato-portal glucose sensing, incretin-mediated vagal signaling, and direct central glucose sensing. In healthy physiology, these excursions are buffered by intact baroreflexes and parasympathetic counterregulation, limiting glucose-HR coherence to brief postprandial windows. In diabetes, impaired autonomic buffering (vagal denervation progresses before sympathetic) allows glucose excursions to drive HR more persistently at 1-4h meal timescales. However, the gross circadian organization of HR (sleep-related bradycardia, daytime tachycardia) is preserved until advanced autonomic neuropathy, so circadian-scale coherence should not differ as strongly. Sub-30-minute fluctuations are dominated by HR noise from posture and activity rather than glucose-driven physiology.
predictions: Wavelet coherence at 1-4h periods shows the largest Cohen's d (>0.6) for healthy-vs-insulin contrast, exceeding the broadband zero-lag correlation effect (d=0.585)
Coherence at <30min periods shows Cohen's d < 0.2 (negative control: noise-dominated scale)
Coherence at >8h circadian periods shows Cohen's d < 0.3 (preserved gross day-night organization)
The 1-4h coherence effect survives adjustment for HbA1c, BMI, mean glucose, mean HR, and activity volume
Within the insulin-dependent group, 1-4h coherence correlates positively with HOMA-IR (r > 0.15)

literature.title: Glucose and unstructured physical activity coupling during sleep and wake in young adults with type 1 diabetes
literature.key_finding: Wavelet coherence between glucose and physical activity was strongest at 120-340 min periods (ultradian timescale) with significant circadian modulation of coupling strength.
literature.relevance: Demonstrates that glucose-activity coupling is timescale-selective in T1D; we hypothesize glucose-HR coupling in T2D has analogous scale dependence.

literature.title: Decreased complexity of glucose dynamics in diabetes: evidence from multiscale entropy analysis of continuous glucose monitoring system data
literature.journal: American Journal of Physiology - Endocrinology and Metabolism
literature.key_finding: Glucose complexity loss in diabetes is scale-dependent, most prominent at scales from 5 min to 5 hours, not explained by mean/variance differences.
literature.relevance: Establishes that diabetes alters glucose dynamics in a scale-dependent manner, supporting the hypothesis that coupling changes are also scale-selective.

literature.title: Network physiology reveals relations between network topology and physiological function
literature.key_finding: Inter-organ coupling strength and topology depend on physiological state (sleep stage) and operate at specific timescales.
literature.relevance: Foundational network physiology framework predicting that coupling breakdown is scale-specific, not broadband.

feasibility.statistical_power: N~1900 with 10-day window; well-powered for d>0.3 across frequency bands
key_challenges: Morlet wavelet coherence requires sufficient time-series length for low-frequency bands
CGM 5-min sampling limits high-frequency resolution
Need cone-of-influence correction for edge effects at multi-day boundaries
dataset_limitations: Garmin HR is not beat-to-beat; high-frequency HR dynamics are smoothed
No medication data to adjust for beta-blocker dampening of HR response
10-day window limits precision of >8h frequency estimates

test_plan.primary_method: Continuous wavelet transform coherence (Morlet wavelet, omega0=6) between glucose and HR, averaged over the 10-day window, computed at 5 frequency bands: <30min, 30-60min, 1-2h, 2-4h, 4-8h, >8h
implementation_steps: Step 1: Load aligned 5-min glucose and HR time series per participant
Step 2: Apply continuous wavelet transform (CWT) with Morlet wavelet to both signals
Step 3: Compute wavelet coherence (WCO) and phase as a function of time and period
Step 4: Average WCO within 6 predefined period bands across time, excluding cone of influence
Step 5: Extract per-participant band-specific mean coherence and mean phase angle
Step 6: Test group differences (Kruskal-Wallis, trend test) for each band separately
Step 7: Compare Cohen's d across bands to test scale-selectivity prediction
Step 8: Run sensitivity models adjusting for age, site, HbA1c, BMI, mean glucose, mean HR
test_plan.expected_effect_size: Cohen's d 0.6-0.8 at 1-4h band; d < 0.2 at <30min band
test_plan.success_criterion: Statistically significant interaction between frequency band and diabetes severity, with 1-4h band showing largest group difference
test_plan.refutation_criterion: If coupling increase is uniform across all frequency bands (no band x group interaction), the timescale-selectivity claim fails. If <30min band shows equal or larger d than 1-4h band, the mechanism is non-specific.
sensitivity_checks: Stratify by awake/sleep to test circadian modulation of the band-specific effect
Bootstrap 1000x per-participant coherence estimates for CI
Compare Morlet vs. Paul wavelet to assess wavelet choice sensitivity
Exclude participants with <5 days of aligned data
secondary_methods: Phase coherence angle distribution (circular statistics)
Hilbert transform instantaneous phase for narrowband signals

notes: This decomposes the broadband coupling finding (H-MIG01) by frequency. If confirmed, the 1-4h band coherence becomes a more mechanistically specific biomarker than the broadband correlation.

title: Asymmetric causal direction: glucose drives HR more than HR drives glucose in diabetes
statement: In healthy individuals, the causal influence between glucose and HR is approximately symmetric (glucose->HR and HR->glucose transfer entropy are similar in magnitude). With increasing diabetes severity, the glucose->HR direction strengthens while the HR->glucose direction weakens, creating a net asymmetry. This reflects the shift from bidirectional autonomic-metabolic coordination to a unidirectional 'glucose dominates HR' regime caused by autonomic neuropathy.
mechanism: In healthy physiology, glucose and HR are bidirectionally coupled: glucose excursions trigger autonomic HR adjustments (glucose->HR), while exercise-driven HR increases mobilize glucose and improve insulin sensitivity (HR->glucose via activity-metabolism coupling). As diabetes progresses, autonomic neuropathy selectively damages the efferent parasympathetic limb first, then sympathetic fibers. The afferent sensing of glucose (hepato-portal, central) remains partially intact, preserving glucose->HR drive via residual sympathetic activation. However, the HR->glucose pathway (exercise-mediated glucose uptake regulation, autonomic modulation of hepatic glucose output) becomes impaired. The net result is an asymmetric causal architecture where glucose is the 'driver' and HR is the 'follower'.
predictions: Transfer entropy (TE) from glucose->HR exceeds TE from HR->glucose in the insulin-dependent group (asymmetry ratio > 1.5)
In healthy participants, the asymmetry ratio is near 1.0 (symmetric coupling)
The asymmetry ratio increases monotonically with diabetes severity (d > 0.3 for linear trend)
Convergent cross mapping (CCM) skill from glucose->HR exceeds CCM skill from HR->glucose in diabetes
The TE asymmetry survives adjustment for activity state (awake/sleep) and mean glucose level
Negative control: TE between glucose and circularly-shifted HR (shifted by >2h) should show no asymmetry

literature.title: Detecting Causality in Complex Ecosystems
literature.key_finding: Convergent cross mapping can detect causal relationships in nonlinear coupled systems even with bidirectional causation, unlike Granger causality.
literature.relevance: CCM is the methodological backbone for testing directed coupling between glucose and HR in a nonlinear physiological system.

literature.title: Cardiac autonomic neuropathy measured by heart rate variability and markers of subclinical atherosclerosis in early type 2 diabetes
literature.key_finding: Reduced HRV in early T2D reflects autonomic neuropathy that precedes overt cardiovascular disease.
literature.relevance: Supports the mechanistic basis that autonomic efferent damage creates asymmetric coupling by impairing the HR->glucose pathway.

literature.title: Disruption of multisystem responses to stress in type 2 diabetes: investigating the dynamics of allostatic load
literature.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
literature.key_finding: T2D shows attenuated post-stress recovery in HR, BP, cortisol, and cholesterol, consistent with impaired autonomic feedback loops.
literature.relevance: Demonstrates that diabetes disrupts bidirectional stress-response dynamics, supporting asymmetric causal architecture.

feasibility.analysis_timescale: acute (5-120 min lags for TE estimation)
feasibility.statistical_power: N~1900 participants x ~2880 timepoints each; sufficient embedding dimension for TE/CCM
key_challenges: Transfer entropy estimation requires careful embedding dimension and lag selection
CCM requires sufficient library length (>500 points per participant available)
Need surrogate data tests to establish significance of individual TE values
Garmin HR sampling may smooth genuine high-frequency causal dynamics
dataset_limitations: No beat-to-beat HR precludes fine-grained causal timing analysis
Activity confounds both glucose and HR; must condition on activity state
Medication effects on HR responsiveness are unobservable

test_plan.primary_method: Transfer entropy (kernel-density or KSG estimator) with embedding dimension selected by false nearest neighbors, computed bidirectionally between glucose and HR for each participant
implementation_steps: Step 1: Load aligned 5-min glucose and HR per participant; standardize each signal to zero mean, unit variance
Step 2: Determine optimal embedding dimension (E) and lag (tau) using simplex projection on glucose and HR separately
Step 3: Compute TE(glucose->HR) and TE(HR->glucose) using KSG estimator with E and tau from step 2, over lags 1-24 steps (5-120 min)
Step 4: Compute asymmetry index: AI = (TE_G->H - TE_H->G) / (TE_G->H + TE_H->G)
Step 5: Validate with surrogate test: compute TE on 100 time-shifted surrogates per participant to establish significance
Step 6: As secondary method, compute CCM skill in both directions with increasing library length
Step 7: Test group differences in AI across diabetes severity groups
Step 8: Run sensitivity analysis conditioning on awake vs sleep, and adjusting for age/site/HbA1c/BMI
test_plan.expected_effect_size: Cohen's d 0.3-0.5 for asymmetry index across severity gradient
test_plan.success_criterion: Significant monotonic increase in glucose->HR dominance (positive AI) with diabetes severity, surviving covariate adjustment
test_plan.refutation_criterion: If AI does not differ across groups (symmetric coupling at all severity levels), or if HR->glucose dominates in diabetes (opposite direction), the hypothesis fails. If surrogate tests show most individual TE values are non-significant, the method has insufficient sensitivity.
sensitivity_checks: Vary embedding dimension E from 2 to 6
Compare KSG vs binning-based TE estimator
Stratify by awake vs sleep periods separately
Condition on activity log-steps as a third variable in conditional TE
Bootstrap 500x for CI on group-level AI differences
secondary_methods: Convergent cross mapping (CCM)
PCMCI with conditional independence tests
Granger causality (linear benchmark)

notes: This extends H-MIG01 from correlation to directed causality. High computational cost but high novelty. Should pilot on 50 participants first to validate TE estimation feasibility at 5-min resolution.

title: Post-excursion HR recovery is prolonged and stereotyped in diabetes
statement: Following glucose excursions (defined as glucose rising >30 mg/dL above the preceding 2-hour mean), HR shows a characteristic post-excursion response: an initial rise followed by a return to baseline. In insulin-dependent diabetes, the HR response amplitude is larger, the peak latency is shorter (faster sympathetic activation), and the recovery time is longer (impaired parasympathetic restoration), compared to healthy controls. Furthermore, the response becomes more stereotyped (lower inter-excursion variability) in diabetes, reflecting loss of context-dependent autonomic modulation.
mechanism: Glucose excursions activate sympathetic outflow through central glucose sensing (area postrema, hypothalamus) and hepato-portal glucose sensors. In health, the baroreceptor reflex and vagal tone rapidly counteract the sympathetic drive, producing variable HR responses depending on concurrent activity, posture, and time of day. In diabetes with autonomic neuropathy, vagal damage reduces the ability to buffer sympathetic HR acceleration, leading to larger and longer HR responses. Additionally, the loss of vagal tone reduces context-dependent modulation of the response, making it more stereotyped. The faster peak latency reflects unopposed sympathetic activation without parasympathetic competition.
predictions: Mean post-excursion HR increase (area under the curve, 0-90 min) is larger in insulin-dependent vs healthy (d > 0.4)
Peak HR latency is shorter in insulin-dependent (15-30 min) vs healthy (30-60 min)
HR recovery half-time (time to return to 50% of peak response) is longer in insulin-dependent (d > 0.3)
Inter-excursion coefficient of variation of HR response amplitude is lower in insulin-dependent (more stereotyped, d > 0.25)
Negative control: randomly selected time windows (not excursion-triggered) should show no group difference in HR response shape
The effect is strongest during waking hours and attenuated during sleep (when excursion-driven HR responses are dampened)

literature.title: Multimodal AI correlates of glucose spikes in people with normal glucose regulation, pre-diabetes and type 2 diabetes
literature.key_finding: Glucose spike resolution time differs systematically by diabetes status; spike dynamics are multimodal predictors of glycemic health beyond mean glucose.
literature.relevance: Establishes that spike dynamics (including resolution time) carry diagnostic information; we extend this to the HR response to spikes.

literature.title: Disruption of multisystem responses to stress in type 2 diabetes
literature.key_finding: Post-stress HR recovery is attenuated in T2D, consistent with impaired parasympathetic reactivation.
literature.relevance: Directly supports the prediction that post-excursion HR recovery is prolonged in diabetes.

literature.title: Loss of 'complexity' and aging: potential applications of fractals and chaos theory to senescence
literature.key_finding: Aging and disease reduce physiological complexity, leading to more stereotyped, less context-dependent responses.
literature.relevance: Grounds the prediction that excursion responses become more stereotyped (reduced inter-excursion variability) in diabetes.

feasibility.statistical_power: N~1900, expect 10-30 excursions per person over 10 days; total events >30,000
key_challenges: Need robust excursion detection algorithm (threshold-based with debouncing)
Must separate meal-driven vs spontaneous excursions (no meal log available)
Activity during excursion window confounds HR response
Garmin HR smoothing may dampen true peak HR response
dataset_limitations: No meal timing data to confirm excursion etiology
No medication timing to account for insulin bolus effects
Garmin HR is averaged/interpolated, not beat-to-beat

test_plan.primary_method: Event-triggered averaging: identify glucose excursions, extract HR in [-30, +90] min windows, compute per-person average response profile and derived metrics (AUC, peak latency, recovery half-time, inter-event CV)
implementation_steps: Step 1: Define glucose excursion as glucose rising >30 mg/dL above the rolling 2-hour mean within a 60-min window
Step 2: Exclude excursions within 120 min of a previous excursion (debounce)
Step 3: For each excursion, extract HR in [-30, +90] min window relative to excursion onset
Step 4: Baseline-subtract HR (subtract mean HR in [-30, 0] min pre-excursion window)
Step 5: Compute per-person: mean response profile, peak amplitude, peak latency, AUC(0-90), recovery half-time, inter-excursion CV of peak amplitude
Step 6: Generate negative control: same analysis at randomly selected non-excursion timepoints
Step 7: Test group differences in each metric across diabetes severity groups
Step 8: Stratify by awake/sleep, adjust for age/site/HbA1c/BMI/excursion magnitude
test_plan.time_window: [-30, +90] min relative to glucose excursion onset
test_plan.expected_effect_size: Cohen's d 0.3-0.5 for HR AUC and recovery time; d 0.25-0.35 for inter-excursion CV
test_plan.success_criterion: FDR-significant group differences in at least 2 of: peak amplitude, peak latency, recovery half-time, inter-excursion CV
test_plan.refutation_criterion: No significant group differences in any excursion-triggered HR metric after adjusting for excursion magnitude and activity. Negative control (random windows) showing equal or larger group differences.
sensitivity_checks: Vary excursion threshold from 20 to 50 mg/dL
Stratify by daytime (8am-8pm) vs nighttime excursions
Exclude excursions during high activity (>100 steps in preceding 30 min)
Bootstrap 1000x per-person excursion averages
Adjust for number of excursions per person (persons with more excursions may differ systematically)
secondary_methods: Gaussian process regression of response profiles per group
Functional data analysis (FDA) of response curves

notes: This tests whether the broadband coupling effect (H-MIG01) is driven by specific event dynamics. High clinical relevance: post-excursion HR recovery could be a practical autonomic neuropathy screening marker.

title: Circadian phase misalignment between glucose and HR rhythms widens with diabetes severity
statement: Glucose and HR each exhibit circadian rhythms (cosinor-detectable 24h periodicity). In healthy individuals, the glucose circadian peak slightly leads the HR circadian peak (glucose peaks ~1-2h after the morning cortisol surge; HR peaks later with daytime activity). In diabetes, the phase relationship between these two rhythms becomes misaligned: the glucose circadian phase advances (earlier glucose rise from impaired dawn phenomenon regulation and hepatic glucose overproduction) while the HR circadian phase is preserved, widening the phase gap. This circadian glucose-HR phase misalignment increases monotonically with diabetes severity.
mechanism: The circadian system coordinates glucose metabolism (via SCN -> hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis -> cortisol -> hepatic glucose output) and autonomic tone (via SCN -> sympathetic/parasympathetic balance -> HR). In healthy physiology, these are phase-locked. In diabetes, hepatic insulin resistance causes exaggerated dawn phenomenon (early morning glucose surge), while the central clock's control of HR circadian rhythm is relatively preserved through non-insulin-dependent pathways. This creates a progressive decoupling of the circadian phase alignment between glucose and HR as insulin resistance and autonomic neuropathy advance. Additionally, disrupted sleep patterns in diabetes (more fragmented, shifted timing) further disrupt the phase relationship.
predictions: Cosinor-fitted circadian glucose acrophase occurs earlier (by 0.5-2 hours) in insulin-dependent vs healthy participants
Cosinor-fitted circadian HR acrophase does not differ as strongly across groups
The glucose-HR phase difference (glucose acrophase minus HR acrophase) changes monotonically with diabetes severity (d > 0.3)
Phase misalignment correlates with HOMA-IR (r > 0.12) after age/site adjustment, reflecting the insulin resistance mechanism

Negative control: glucose-activity phase difference should track diabetes severity less strongly than glucose-HR phase difference, because activity patterns are behaviorally determined rather than autonomically driven

literature.title: Adverse metabolic and cardiovascular consequences of circadian misalignment
literature.key_finding: Controlled circadian misalignment causes glucose intolerance, elevated BP, and altered cortisol rhythms, demonstrating that phase misalignment directly impairs metabolism.
literature.relevance: Establishes the causal link between circadian phase disruption and metabolic dysfunction; we test whether this manifests as glucose-HR phase misalignment in free-living diabetes.

literature.title: Circadian clock, diurnal glucose metabolic rhythm, and dawn phenomenon
literature.key_finding: The dawn phenomenon reflects circadian-regulated hepatic glucose output that becomes exaggerated in diabetes due to insulin resistance.
literature.relevance: Supports the mechanism that glucose circadian phase advances in diabetes while HR phase is preserved.

literature.title: Impact of circadian disruption on glucose metabolism: implications for type 2 diabetes
literature.key_finding: Circadian disruption from mistimed light, sleep, or food intake worsens glycemic control through multiple coordinated pathways.
literature.relevance: Provides the broader framework linking circadian misalignment to diabetes progression.

feasibility.statistical_power: N~1900 with 10 days of data; cosinor fits are robust with >7 days
key_challenges: Cosinor model assumes sinusoidal 24h rhythm which may be imperfect for glucose (multi-peak from meals)
Need to verify cosinor goodness-of-fit (R2) is sufficient per participant before extracting phase
Phase estimation from 10 days is more reliable than single-day but still limited
dataset_limitations: No meal timing to separate endogenous circadian glucose from postprandial effects
Sleep timing variability (social jetlag) is a confounder
10-day window limits precision of circadian phase estimation vs longer studies

test_plan.primary_method: Cosinor analysis: fit 24h cosinor model to glucose and HR time series per participant, extract acrophase, amplitude, and mesor. Compute phase difference. Test group trend.
implementation_steps: Step 1: Compute hourly means of glucose and HR per participant over full 10-day window
Step 2: Fit single-component cosinor model (24h period) to each signal per participant
Step 3: Extract acrophase (peak time), amplitude, mesor, and goodness-of-fit for each signal
Step 4: Filter to participants with cosinor R2 > 0.1 for both signals (sufficient rhythmicity)
Step 5: Compute glucose-HR phase difference (circular subtraction)
Step 6: Test group differences in phase difference using circular ANOVA (Watson-Williams test)
Step 7: Test linear trend with severity using circular-linear correlation
Step 8: Correlate phase difference with HOMA-IR, frailty index, allostatic load after age/site adjustment
test_plan.expected_effect_size: Phase difference shift of 0.5-2 hours; Cohen's d 0.3-0.5 for severity trend
test_plan.success_criterion: FDR-significant circadian phase misalignment between glucose and HR that increases with diabetes severity and correlates with insulin resistance markers
test_plan.refutation_criterion: No group difference in glucose-HR phase relationship. Glucose and HR acrophases shift in parallel (preserved phase coupling). Phase difference unrelated to HOMA-IR.
sensitivity_checks: Use two-component cosinor (24h + 12h harmonics) to handle non-sinusoidal waveforms
Stratify by weekday vs weekend to assess social jetlag effects
Compare phase from first 5 days vs last 5 days for stability
Exclude participants with irregular sleep schedules (high sleep onset variability)
secondary_methods: Lomb-Scargle periodogram for rhythm detection
Cross-correlation at 24h lag to assess circadian coupling strength

notes: Complements H-NEW01 by specifically testing the circadian timescale. If cosinor R2 is too low for many participants, consider switching to Lomb-Scargle or wavelet-based circadian phase extraction.

title: Glucose complexity loss at 1-3 hour scales predicts allostatic load beyond HbA1c
statement: Multiscale sample entropy of CGM glucose at 1-3 hour timescales (scales 12-36 at 5-min resolution) is lower in diabetes and independently predicts allostatic load and frailty index after adjusting for HbA1c, BMI, age, and site. This glucose complexity metric captures regulatory capacity (the ability to maintain non-repetitive, adaptive glucose fluctuations) that degrades with multisystem physiological burden and is not captured by mean glucose or HbA1c.
mechanism: Healthy glucose regulation involves multiple interacting feedback loops operating at different timescales: rapid insulin secretion (minutes), incretin responses (30-60 min), counterregulatory hormones (1-3 hours), and hepatic glucose cycling (2-4 hours). These overlapping controllers produce complex, non-repetitive glucose dynamics with high multiscale entropy. As diabetes progresses, these controllers fail sequentially: first-phase insulin secretion is lost, then incretin amplification, then counterregulatory coordination. The loss of controller diversity reduces the complexity of glucose dynamics specifically at 1-3 hour scales where these controllers overlap. Because allostatic load and frailty reflect multisystem regulatory failure (not just glycemia), glucose complexity at these scales should capture shared regulatory degradation beyond what HbA1c measures.
predictions: Formal sample entropy (SampEn) at scales 12-36 (1-3h) is lower in insulin-dependent vs healthy (d > 0.4)
SampEn at these scales predicts allostatic load (partial r > 0.10) after adjusting for age, site, HbA1c, BMI
SampEn at these scales predicts frailty index (partial r > 0.10) after the same adjustment
The existing Shannon entropy proxy (from coupling_features.py) at scale 3 and scale 12 shows a similar pattern but weaker than formal SampEn
Negative control: glucose mean and glucose SD do NOT predict allostatic load after HbA1c adjustment (complexity adds information beyond level/variability)
Entropy at very short scales (scale 1, 5 min) is weaker because it is dominated by sensor noise

literature.title: Decreased complexity of glucose dynamics in diabetes: evidence from multiscale entropy analysis of continuous glucose monitoring system data
literature.journal: American Journal of Physiology - Endocrinology and Metabolism
literature.key_finding: Glucose MSE is lower in diabetes across scales from 5 min to 5 hours; the effect is not explained by mean or range differences.
literature.relevance: Directly establishes that glucose complexity loss is measurable from CGM and scale-dependent; we extend to clinical outcome prediction.

literature.title: Dynamical glucometry: Use of multiscale entropy analysis in diabetes
literature.key_finding: Proposed MSE as a clinical CGM metric ('dynamical glucometry') complementing mean glucose and variability measures.
literature.relevance: Establishes the analytical framework; we test whether the metric has clinical utility for predicting systemic burden.

literature.title: Multiscale entropy analysis of complex physiologic time series
literature.key_finding: Introduced MSE methodology showing that pathological states reduce complexity across scales, not just at single scales.
literature.relevance: Foundational method paper for MSE applied to physiological time series.

feasibility.statistical_power: N~2200 with CGM data; well-powered for r>0.10 partial correlations
key_challenges: Formal sample entropy requires parameter selection (m, r) and is sensitive to time-series length
CGM gaps require interpolation or segmentation strategy
Must distinguish between complexity loss from disease vs from CGM sensor artifacts
dataset_limitations: No medication data: metformin and insulin both affect glucose dynamics independently of disease biology
CGM sensor drift/calibration may mimic or mask complexity changes
The existing Shannon entropy proxy in coupling_features.py is NOT formal SampEn; need to implement proper SampEn

test_plan.primary_method: Multiscale sample entropy (MSE) computed for each participant's glucose time series at scales 1,3,6,12,18,24,36,72 (5min to 6h). Test group trends and partial correlations with clinical outcomes.
implementation_steps: Step 1: Load CGM glucose for each participant, interpolate gaps <30 min, exclude participants with <1500 valid 5-min points (5.2 days)
Step 2: Compute formal sample entropy (SampEn) with m=2, r=0.15*SD at each scale via coarse-graining
Step 3: Compute complexity index (CI) as area under the MSE curve for scales 12-36 (1-3h)
Step 4: Test group trend in CI and per-scale SampEn across diabetes severity
Step 5: Fit partial correlation models: CI ~ allostatic_load, adjusting for age, site, HbA1c, BMI
Step 6: Same for frailty index, homeostatic dysregulation, HOMA-IR
Step 7: Compare incremental R2 from adding CI to a base model (age+site+HbA1c+BMI) predicting each outcome
Step 8: Negative control: test glucose_mean and glucose_SD as predictors of allostatic load after HbA1c adjustment
test_plan.expected_effect_size: Cohen's d 0.4-0.6 for CI group trend; partial r 0.10-0.15 for CI vs allostatic load after HbA1c adjustment
test_plan.success_criterion: CI independently predicts allostatic load and frailty after HbA1c/BMI/age/site adjustment (FDR p < 0.01), and glucose mean/SD do not survive the same adjustment
test_plan.refutation_criterion: CI does not predict any clinical outcome after HbA1c adjustment. CI is fully explained by glucose mean and glucose SD. The existing Shannon entropy proxy already captures the full signal.
sensitivity_checks: Vary SampEn parameters: m={1,2,3}, r={0.10,0.15,0.20}*SD
Compare formal SampEn vs approximate entropy (ApEn) vs fuzzy entropy
Stratify by CGM data completeness (>80% vs <80%)
Test stability: first 5 days vs last 5 days
Cross-validate: train incremental R2 on train set, evaluate on test set
secondary_methods: Detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) for fractal scaling exponent
Permutation entropy as a complementary complexity measure

notes: Directly extends the existing Shannon entropy proxy in coupling_features.py with formal sample entropy. If the Shannon proxy already captures most of the signal, formal SampEn may not add much. Test both.

title: Nocturnal glucose-HR coupling predicts next-day glycemic control
statement: Within each participant, nights with stronger (more positive) glucose-HR coupling during the sleep period are followed by days with worse glycemic control (higher mean glucose, lower time in range, higher glycemic variability). This night-to-day predictive relationship is stronger in the diabetes groups than in healthy controls, because in diabetes the nocturnal autonomic-metabolic linkage reflects overnight hepatic glucose overproduction and impaired dawn phenomenon regulation that carry forward into daytime glycemia.
mechanism: During sleep, glucose dynamics are primarily driven by endogenous processes: hepatic glucose output regulated by glucagon, growth hormone, and cortisol surges (dawn phenomenon), and residual insulin action. HR during sleep reflects basal autonomic tone. In healthy individuals, nocturnal glucose and HR are weakly coupled because hepatic glucose output and sleep-stage autonomic modulation operate independently. In diabetes, impaired suppression of hepatic glucose output (insulin resistance) creates overnight hyperglycemia that triggers persistent sympathetic activation, producing glucose-HR co-elevation. Nights where this coupling is strongest reflect the most active hepatic overproduction, which carries forward into the following daytime as elevated fasting glucose, reduced time in range, and greater excursion frequency.
predictions: Night-level glucose-HR correlation (computed per sleep period) predicts next-day mean glucose (r > 0.15 within-person) in the diabetes groups
This within-person predictive relationship is weaker in healthy controls (r < 0.05)
The diabetes vs healthy difference in this predictive strength is significant (interaction p < 0.01)
The effect is mediated partly through morning fasting glucose (dawn phenomenon amplitude)
Negative control: daytime glucose-HR coupling does not predict next-day glycemia as strongly as nocturnal coupling

literature.title: Slow-oscillation/spindle coupling predicts next-day fasting glucose in adults with type 2 diabetes
literature.key_finding: Sleep microstructure coupling (SO-spindle) predicts next-morning fasting glucose, partly mediated by autonomic activity during sleep.
literature.relevance: Establishes the night-to-day predictive framework; we use macrostructural glucose-HR coupling instead of EEG microstructure (which AI-READI lacks).

literature.title: Effects of night-to-night variations in objectively measured sleep on blood glucose in healthy university students
literature.key_finding: Longer sleep duration associated with lower same-night glucose variability, but no significant effect on next-day glucose in healthy young adults.
literature.relevance: Supports the prediction that the night-to-day effect is diabetes-specific, not present in healthy individuals.

literature.title: Dawn Phenomenon
literature.key_finding: Dawn phenomenon affects >50% of people with diabetes, is driven by cortisol/GH surges and hepatic insulin resistance, and is detectable via CGM.
literature.relevance: Provides the mechanism linking nocturnal glucose dynamics to morning/daytime glycemic control.

feasibility.statistical_power: N~1500 participants with sleep data x ~8 night-day pairs each = ~12,000 night-day observations for mixed-effects models
key_challenges: Garmin sleep staging quality limits precision of sleep period detection
Within-person night-to-night variability may be low over 10 days
Must use mixed-effects models to separate within-person from between-person effects
dataset_limitations: Consumer-grade sleep staging; sleep periods may be misclassified
10 days yields only ~8-9 night-day pairs per person; limited for individual-level models
No medication timing data to separate medication effects from endogenous dawn phenomenon

test_plan.primary_method: Mixed-effects regression: next-day glycemic metric ~ nocturnal glucose-HR coupling + random intercept per participant, with group interaction term for diabetes severity
implementation_steps: Step 1: Segment each participant's data into night periods (using sleep start/end from Garmin) and subsequent day periods
Step 2: For each night, compute glucose-HR Pearson correlation during sleep period
Step 3: For each subsequent day (sleep end to next sleep start), compute: mean glucose, TIR (70-180), glucose SD, glucose CV
Step 4: Fit mixed-effects model: next_day_mean_glucose ~ nocturnal_glucose_hr_r + (1|person_id)
Step 5: Add group interaction: ~ nocturnal_glucose_hr_r * study_group + covariates + (1|person_id)
Step 6: Test whether the interaction term (coupling x severity) is significant
Step 7: Negative control: same model with daytime glucose-HR coupling predicting next-day glycemia
Step 8: Mediation analysis: test whether morning fasting glucose (first 30-min post-waking) mediates the effect

title: Evening light exposure amplifies overnight glucose-HR coupling in diabetes
statement: Higher evening light exposure (measured by the environmental sensor in the 3 hours before sleep onset) amplifies overnight glucose-HR coupling specifically in the diabetes groups but not in healthy controls. This occurs because evening light suppresses melatonin, which impairs insulin secretion and exacerbates nocturnal hepatic glucose output. The resulting hyperglycemia drives sympathetic activation, strengthening glucose-HR coupling. In healthy individuals, intact insulin reserves compensate for melatonin suppression, preventing the coupling amplification.
mechanism: Melatonin is secreted by the pineal gland in darkness and acts on pancreatic beta cells to modulate insulin secretion timing. Evening light exposure suppresses melatonin, shifting insulin secretion timing and reducing its overnight efficacy. In individuals with intact beta-cell function (healthy), this suppression is compensated by increased basal insulin secretion. In diabetes, where beta-cell reserve is diminished and hepatic insulin resistance is present, melatonin suppression removes a secondary brake on overnight hepatic glucose output, leading to greater nocturnal hyperglycemia. This hyperglycemia triggers sympathetic activation via central glucose sensing, strengthening the glucose-HR coupling signal. The AI-READI environmental sensor captures ambient light levels that can serve as a proxy for light exposure.
predictions: Within-person: nights preceded by higher evening light (top tertile vs bottom tertile of 3h pre-sleep light) show stronger glucose-HR coupling during sleep in diabetes groups
This light-coupling interaction is absent or weak in healthy controls
The light-coupling amplification effect increases with diabetes severity (group x light interaction)
The effect is stronger for short-wavelength-enriched light (if spectrum data available) than long-wavelength light
Negative control: evening temperature and humidity do not modulate overnight glucose-HR coupling similarly

title: Coupling-defined physiotypes capture distinct metabolic phenotypes missed by HbA1c stratification
statement: Unsupervised clustering on dynamic coupling features (glucose-HR, glucose-activity, sleep-glucose, complexity metrics) reveals 3-5 distinct physiotypes that cross-cut HbA1c-based diabetes severity categories. Specifically, there exist individuals with high HbA1c but normal coupling patterns (preserved regulatory physiology despite hyperglycemia, possibly medication-controlled) and individuals with normal HbA1c but abnormal coupling (early dysregulation not yet reflected in mean glycemia). These coupling-defined physiotypes predict frailty index and allostatic load better than HbA1c quartiles alone.
mechanism: HbA1c reflects the average glycemic level over 2-3 months but does not capture the dynamic organization of physiological regulation. Two individuals with identical HbA1c may differ in: (1) the complexity of their glucose dynamics, (2) the autonomic responsiveness of their HR to glucose excursions, (3) the circadian coordination of their metabolic rhythms, and (4) the coupling of activity to glucose regulation. These dynamic properties reflect the state of multiple regulatory systems (pancreatic, hepatic, autonomic, circadian, behavioral) that collectively determine health trajectory. Clustering on coupling features should capture this regulatory phenotype space, identifying groups defined by physiological organization rather than average glycemic level.
predictions: K-means or spectral clustering on coupling features yields 3-5 stable clusters with silhouette score > 0.15
Clusters are NOT aligned with HbA1c quartiles: Adjusted Rand Index between cluster labels and HbA1c quartiles < 0.15
At least one cluster contains participants from both healthy and diabetes groups (HbA1c-discordant physiotype)
Coupling-based clusters predict frailty index variance better than HbA1c quartiles (incremental R2 > 0.03)

Clusters have distinct clinical profiles (e.g., one cluster may have high glucose complexity + high coupling = pre-clinical dysregulation; another may have low complexity + normal coupling = stable but rigid)

title: Glucose-HR coupling links to retinal OCTA vessel density through shared autonomic damage
statement: While broadband glucose-HR coupling does not predict retinal age acceleration (H-MIG05, refuted), a more specific test should reveal a link: coupling features that specifically index autonomic neuropathy (glucose->HR transfer entropy asymmetry, post-excursion HR recovery time) predict retinal superficial vessel density (SVD) loss measured by OCTA, after adjusting for age, HbA1c, and BMI. This is because both autonomic HR dysfunction and retinal microvascular rarefaction share a common upstream cause: small-vessel and nerve damage from chronic hyperglycemia and oxidative stress.
mechanism: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy and diabetic retinal microvasculopathy share common pathogenic mechanisms: hyperglycemia-driven advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), polyol pathway activation, oxidative stress, and pericyte loss. The autonomic nerve fibers that regulate HR are small unmyelinated (vagal) and small myelinated (sympathetic) fibers vulnerable to the same microvascular ischemia that damages retinal capillaries. OCTA-measured superficial vessel density directly reflects capillary dropout in the retinal ganglion cell layer, which is one of the earliest structural changes in diabetic retinopathy. If glucose-HR coupling features reflect autonomic damage, and retinal vessel density reflects microvascular damage, and both share the same upstream cause, then there should be a detectable partial correlation between autonomic-specific coupling features and retinal vessel density after adjusting for glycemic level.
predictions: Post-excursion HR recovery time (from H-NEW03) correlates negatively with OCTA superficial vessel density (partial r -0.08 to -0.15 after age/HbA1c/BMI/site adjustment)
Glucose->HR transfer entropy asymmetry (from H-NEW02) correlates negatively with SVD (shared autonomic-microvascular damage)
Broadband glucose-HR coupling (awake_r) does NOT correlate with SVD after adjustment (confirming H-MIG05 and showing that autonomic-specific features are needed)
The coupling-SVD link is present in the diabetes groups but absent in healthy (interaction effect)
Negative control: glucose-activity coupling does NOT predict SVD (activity coupling is behavioral, not autonomic)

title: Activity-glucose coupling direction reverses between exercise and recovery phases
statement: During acute activity bouts (sustained elevated step count for >15 min), glucose typically decreases in healthy individuals due to skeletal muscle glucose uptake (activity drives glucose DOWN). During the 1-3 hour recovery period after exercise cessation, glucose may transiently rise (hepatic glucose repletion and counterregulatory hormones), creating a rebound. In diabetes, the exercise-induced glucose decrease is blunted (impaired muscle glucose uptake, insulin resistance) and the post-exercise rebound is exaggerated (hepatic glucose overproduction). This produces a reversal of the activity-glucose coupling direction between exercise and recovery that is more pronounced with diabetes severity.
mechanism: During exercise, insulin-independent glucose uptake by contracting skeletal muscle (via GLUT4 translocation) decreases circulating glucose. Simultaneously, hepatic glucose output increases to match demand, but in healthy individuals muscle uptake exceeds hepatic output, resulting in net glucose decrease. After exercise, muscle uptake decreases rapidly while hepatic output remains elevated (counterregulatory hormones: glucagon, cortisol, catecholamines), causing a transient glucose rebound. In diabetes, skeletal muscle insulin resistance impairs glucose uptake during exercise, and hepatic insulin resistance causes exaggerated post-exercise glucose output. This reduces the during-exercise glucose drop and amplifies the post-exercise rebound, creating a more asymmetric and potentially reversed coupling pattern.
predictions: During activity bouts, activity-glucose correlation is more negative (larger glucose decrease per step) in healthy vs insulin-dependent (d > 0.3)
During 1-3h post-activity recovery, activity-glucose correlation reverses to positive (glucose rebound) and this rebound magnitude is larger in insulin-dependent (d > 0.25)
The exercise-recovery coupling asymmetry (difference between during and post coupling) increases with diabetes severity
Negative control: during rest periods (no activity), the activity-glucose coupling is near zero in all groups
The effect is strongest for moderate activity bouts (50-200 steps in 15 min) and less clear for very light activity

title: Day-to-day coupling instability is a resilience marker that predicts clinical burden
statement: The day-to-day variability (instability) of glucose-HR coupling strength is itself a marker of physiological resilience. In healthy individuals, coupling strength varies substantially from day to day because it is context-dependent (meals, activity, sleep quality, stress). In advanced diabetes, coupling becomes rigidly positive every day (loss of context dependence), reducing day-to-day variability. The coefficient of variation (CV) of daily glucose-HR coupling across the 10-day window decreases with diabetes severity and independently predicts frailty index and allostatic load.
mechanism: Day-to-day variability in inter-organ coupling reflects the system's capacity to modulate its internal coordination in response to varying daily demands. In healthy physiology, autonomic reflexes and metabolic flexibility allow glucose-HR coupling to be strong on some days (high carb intake, sedentary) and weak or negative on others (exercise days, fasting). This variability is a signature of adaptive capacity. In diabetes, loss of metabolic flexibility (impaired fuel switching), autonomic rigidity (fixed sympathetic dominance), and reduced behavioral variability (less exercise, more routine) collapse the coupling into a narrow, persistently positive range. This loss of day-to-day coupling variability parallels the loss-of-complexity principle from Lipsitz & Goldberger: disease reduces not just signal complexity but also the variability of inter-signal relationships.
predictions: The CV of daily glucose-HR coupling (computed from ~10 daily estimates per person) decreases with diabetes severity (d > 0.25)
Day-to-day coupling CV independently predicts frailty index (partial r > 0.08) after adjusting for age, site, HbA1c, BMI, and mean coupling level
Day-to-day coupling CV independently predicts allostatic load (partial r > 0.08) after the same adjustment
Negative control: the CV of daily glucose MEAN does not have the same independent predictive power (variability of coupling, not of glucose level, is the marker)
Participants with the lowest day-to-day coupling CV have the highest coupling means (rigid positive coupling = low variability + high mean)

Step 2: Compute Pearson correlation between glucose and HR for each day (require >= 100 valid 5-min points per day, i.e., >8.3 hours)

Step 8: Test correlation between mean coupling and coupling CV (expected negative: high mean = low variability)

title: PM2.5 acutely amplifies glucose-HR coupling through inflammation-mediated autonomic activation
statement: Within-person day-to-day fluctuations in PM2.5 exposure modulate same-day glucose-HR coupling strength: higher PM2.5 days are followed by stronger (more positive) glucose-HR coupling with a 12-24 hour lag, especially in diabetes. This occurs because PM2.5 triggers systemic inflammation (IL-6, TNF-alpha) and oxidative stress that impairs autonomic balance (reducing vagal tone, increasing sympathetic drive), amplifying the pathological glucose-HR locking. The effect is stronger in diabetes because the autonomic system is already compromised and has less reserve to buffer the PM2.5 perturbation.
mechanism: Inhaled PM2.5 triggers alveolar macrophage activation within hours, releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-1beta) into the circulation. These cytokines act on the CNS (via vagal afferents and circumventricular organs) to increase sympathetic outflow and reduce vagal tone. Additionally, PM2.5 particles that enter the bloodstream directly activate endothelial oxidative stress and impair endothelial NO production, further impairing autonomic vasomotor regulation. In healthy individuals, intact autonomic reserve can buffer these perturbations, maintaining relatively decoupled glucose-HR dynamics. In diabetes, where vagal tone is already reduced and sympathetic tone is elevated, the additional PM2.5-induced autonomic shift pushes the system further into pathological glucose-HR locking. The 12-24h lag reflects the time course of systemic inflammation from PM2.5 inhalation to peak cytokine levels and autonomic effects.
predictions: Within-person: days with higher PM2.5 (top tertile) are followed by days with stronger glucose-HR coupling (r increase of 0.02-0.05 at 12-24h lag)
This PM2.5->coupling relationship is stronger in insulin-dependent participants (interaction d > 0.15)
The lag structure shows peak effect at 12-24h (consistent with inflammatory cascade timing), weaker at 0-6h and >36h
Negative control: temperature and humidity fluctuations do not predict coupling changes at the same lag
The effect is attenuated when both PM2.5 and coupling are detrended for time-of-day and day-of-week
