Limited day-to-day PM2.5 variability in some locations (especially controlled indoor environments)
Need within-person detrending to remove between-person confounding
dataset_limitations: Environment sensor measures room-level PM2.5, not personal exposure
PM2.5 composition data not available (total mass only)
10-day window limits the number of day-to-day PM2.5 fluctuations per person

test_plan.primary_method: Within-person lagged mixed-effects model: daily_coupling ~ PM2.5_lag_1d * study_group + covariates + (1|person_id), with person-mean-centered PM2.5
implementation_steps: Step 1: Compute daily mean PM2.5 from environment sensor per participant (excluding missing days)
Step 2: Compute daily glucose-HR coupling (Pearson r, awake-only) per participant
Step 3: Person-mean-center both PM2.5 and coupling to extract within-person fluctuations
Step 4: Fit mixed-effects model with lagged PM2.5 (lag=0, 1, 2 days) predicting coupling
Step 5: Add study_group x PM2.5_lag interaction to test diabetes-specific amplification
Step 6: Test lag structure: compare model fit at lag 0, 1, 2 days
Step 7: Negative controls: replace PM2.5 with temperature and humidity; test same model
Step 8: Sensitivity: add time-of-day and day-of-week fixed effects
test_plan.expected_effect_size: Within-person standardized beta 0.03-0.08 for PM2.5_lag_1d -> coupling; interaction d 0.15-0.25
test_plan.success_criterion: Significant within-person PM2.5 -> coupling association at 12-24h lag (p < 0.01) with diabetes severity interaction
test_plan.refutation_criterion: No within-person PM2.5 -> coupling association at any lag. Temperature/humidity show equal or stronger effects (non-specific). Effect disappears after autocorrelation adjustment.
sensitivity_checks: Use 6h-binned PM2.5 for finer lag resolution
Stratify by site (UAB/UW/UCSD have different air quality environments)
Test PM2.5 variance instead of mean as predictor (spike exposure)
Adjust for autocorrelation in coupling time series (AR(1) model)
Exclude days with very low PM2.5 variance (<2 ug/m3 within-day range)
secondary_methods: Distributed lag nonlinear model (DLNM) for flexible lag-response curves
Conditional Granger causality: PM2.5 -> coupling, conditioning on activity

notes: This is a more rigorous retest of H-MIG06 (which was inconclusive). Key improvements: within-person detrending, lag structure analysis, negative controls, and interaction with diabetes severity. Still limited by indoor PM2.5 measurement.

title: Sleep-wake transition dynamics reveal coupling reorganization speed as a diabetes marker
statement: The transition from sleep to wakefulness requires rapid reorganization of physiological coupling: glucose-HR coupling must shift from sleep-mode (weak, vagally-dominated) to wake-mode (stronger, activity-responsive). In diabetes, this reorganization is slower, taking 30-60 minutes longer to reach stable wake-mode coupling compared to healthy controls (who reorganize within 15-30 minutes of waking). This 'coupling reorganization latency' is a resilience metric that reflects the speed of autonomic mode-switching, which degrades with autonomic neuropathy.
mechanism: The sleep-to-wake transition involves a rapid shift in autonomic balance: vagal withdrawal, sympathetic activation, cortisol surge, and behavioral activation. In healthy individuals, the autonomic nervous system executes this transition rapidly, reflected in quick stabilization of the wake-mode glucose-HR coupling pattern (stronger positive coupling driven by activity-metabolism coordination). In diabetes with autonomic neuropathy, both the vagal withdrawal (already partially denervated) and sympathetic recruitment are sluggish, creating a prolonged transition period where coupling fluctuates between sleep and wake modes. This parallels the known impairment of heart rate recovery after exercise in diabetic autonomic neuropathy, but at the sleep-wake transition.
predictions: Glucose-HR coupling in a sliding 30-min window stabilizes to wake-mode values within 15-30 min of waking in healthy participants
In insulin-dependent participants, stabilization takes 45-90 min (coupling reorganization latency 2-3x longer, d > 0.3)
Reorganization latency increases monotonically with diabetes severity
Negative control: the wake-to-sleep transition latency does not differ as strongly (falling asleep is more passive, less demanding of rapid autonomic mode-switching)
Reorganization latency correlates with clinical RMSSD from ECG (both index vagal function)

literature.title: Network physiology reveals relations between network topology and physiological function
literature.key_finding: Network coupling topology reorganizes between sleep stages within minutes, and the speed of reorganization may be a marker of network health.
literature.relevance: Directly motivates measuring reorganization speed at sleep-wake transitions as a network physiology metric.

literature.title: Heart rate variability for the early detection of cardiac autonomic dysfunction in type 1 diabetes
literature.key_finding: Early autonomic dysfunction in diabetes manifests as impaired HR responsiveness to physiological challenges, detectable before overt neuropathy symptoms.
literature.relevance: Supports the idea that autonomic mode-switching speed (including sleep-wake transitions) degrades early in diabetes.

literature.title: Disruption of multisystem responses to stress in type 2 diabetes
literature.key_finding: Post-stress recovery of HR, BP, and cortisol is attenuated in T2D, reflecting impaired autonomic mode-switching.
literature.relevance: The sleep-wake transition is a natural 'stress' that requires rapid autonomic recovery/reorganization.

feasibility.statistical_power: N~1500 with sleep data x ~8 mornings = ~12,000 waking transitions
key_challenges: Garmin sleep end-time may not precisely mark waking moment
Morning routine variability (bathroom, coffee, breakfast) confounds the transition period
30-min sliding window needs enough points (6 x 5-min = 6 data points) for meaningful correlation
Need to define 'stabilization' operationally (e.g., coupling within 1 SD of 2-hour post-waking mean)
dataset_limitations: Consumer-grade sleep staging; waking time precision is limited
No behavioral log to distinguish 'lying awake in bed' from 'active morning routine'
Only ~8 mornings per person limits per-person averaging

test_plan.primary_method: Sliding-window coupling analysis: compute glucose-HR correlation in 30-min windows sliding by 5 min from 30 min pre-waking to 120 min post-waking. Define reorganization latency as time to reach stable wake-mode coupling.
implementation_steps: Step 1: Identify waking time from Garmin sleep end_time per morning
Step 2: Extract glucose and HR in [-30, +120] min window around waking
Step 3: Compute glucose-HR Pearson r in 30-min sliding windows (step = 5 min)
Step 4: Define wake-mode coupling as mean r from +60 to +120 min post-waking (stable period)
Step 5: Define reorganization latency as time post-waking when sliding-window r first enters and stays within 1 SD of wake-mode value for >= 15 min
Step 6: Average reorganization latency across mornings per person
Step 7: Test group differences in mean reorganization latency
Step 8: Correlate with RMSSD from ECG and with frailty index
test_plan.expected_effect_size: Cohen's d 0.3-0.5 for reorganization latency across severity gradient
test_plan.success_criterion: Reorganization latency increases monotonically with diabetes severity (FDR p < 0.01) and correlates with ECG RMSSD
test_plan.refutation_criterion: No group difference in reorganization latency. Wake-to-sleep transition shows equal or larger group differences (no direction specificity). Reorganization latency is fully explained by waking glucose level.
sensitivity_checks: Vary sliding window width: 20, 30, 45 min
Vary stabilization criterion: 0.5 SD, 1 SD, 1.5 SD of wake-mode value
Test wake-to-sleep transition as negative comparator
Exclude mornings with very early (<5am) or very late (>10am) waking
Compare Garmin-detected waking vs first activity (>10 steps) as waking marker
secondary_methods: Change-point detection (PELT algorithm) on coupling time series at wake transition
Dynamic time warping to align coupling reorganization curves across participants

notes: Novel metric directly inspired by Bashan et al. network reorganization dynamics. The AI-READI dataset uniquely enables this because it has concurrent CGM + HR + sleep staging across the waking transition, which most standalone CGM or wearable studies lack.

title: Cross-recurrence of glucose-HR trajectories reveals attractor convergence in diabetes
statement: Joint glucose-HR dynamics in healthy individuals explore a high-dimensional state space (low determinism in cross-recurrence plots). In diabetes, the joint dynamics collapse onto a low-dimensional attractor (high determinism, high laminarity in cross-recurrence quantification analysis). This reflects the loss of degrees of freedom in the coupled metabolic-autonomic system as regulatory feedback loops fail.
mechanism: In healthy physiology, glucose and HR are influenced by numerous semi-independent controllers: baroreflexes, insulin/glucagon balance, incretin hormones, cortisol, growth hormone, behavioral choices, autonomic tone, and circadian timing. These controllers create a high-dimensional joint dynamics where the glucose-HR trajectory visits many regions of state space non-repetitively. As diabetes damages these controllers (beta-cell failure, autonomic neuropathy, loss of incretin amplification, impaired baroreflexes), the system loses degrees of freedom and the glucose-HR trajectory becomes trapped near a low-dimensional attractor dominated by the surviving glucose->sympathetic->HR pathway. Cross-recurrence quantification analysis (CRQA) directly measures this dimensionality collapse through determinism (DET), laminarity (LAM), and trapping time (TT).
predictions: CRQA determinism (DET) of glucose-HR cross-recurrence increases with diabetes severity (d > 0.3)
CRQA laminarity (LAM) of glucose-HR cross-recurrence increases with diabetes severity (d > 0.25)
CRQA trapping time (TT) increases with diabetes severity (longer sojourns in recurrent states)
CRQA entropy (ENTR, diagonal line length distribution entropy) decreases with severity (fewer distinct recurrence patterns)
Negative control: CRQA metrics from randomly paired glucose-HR (different participants, same site) show no group differences
CRQA DET independently predicts frailty index beyond the broadband glucose-HR correlation

literature.title: Diabetes alters cardiorespiratory dynamics: insights from short-term recurrence quantification analysis of pulse-respiration quotient
literature.key_finding: RQA of cardiorespiratory dynamics shows increased determinism and reduced complexity in diabetic patients.
literature.relevance: Directly demonstrates that RQA detects diabetes-related dynamical changes in physiological coupling.

literature.title: Recurrence Quantification Analysis of Heart Rate Dynamics in Young Patients with Diabetes Mellitus
literature.journal: World Congress on Medical Physics and Biomedical Engineering
literature.key_finding: RQA of heart rate in diabetic youth shows higher recurrence rate, determinism, and trapping time, indicating reduced complexity.
literature.relevance: Establishes that RQA metrics capture diabetes-related HR dynamics changes; we extend to cross-recurrence (glucose x HR).

literature.title: The geometry of synchronization: quantifying the coupling direction of physiological signals of stress
literature.key_finding: Inter-system recurrence networks can detect coupling direction and synchronization patterns in physiological signal pairs.
literature.relevance: Provides the methodological framework for applying cross-recurrence to physiological coupling analysis.

feasibility.analysis_timescale: full 10-day window (CRQA on long time series)
feasibility.statistical_power: N~1900 with ~2880 timepoints each; sufficient for CRQA with embedding dimension 3-5
key_challenges: CRQA parameter selection: embedding dimension, delay, threshold (recurrence rate)
Computational cost: cross-recurrence matrix is N x N where N~2880
Sensitivity to data gaps and non-stationarity
Need to standardize signals before computing recurrence (z-score both glucose and HR)
dataset_limitations: 5-min resolution may not capture fast dynamical transitions
Data gaps require segmentation or interpolation
CRQA is less well-known than correlation/TE methods; reviewers may need education

test_plan.primary_method: Cross-recurrence quantification analysis (CRQA) of glucose-HR time series per participant, with standardized parameter selection protocol
implementation_steps: Step 1: Load aligned 5-min glucose and HR; z-score each signal
Step 2: Determine embedding parameters: E via false nearest neighbors, tau via first minimum of mutual information
Step 3: Compute cross-recurrence matrix with threshold set to achieve 5% recurrence rate
Step 4: Extract CRQA metrics: recurrence rate (RR), determinism (DET), laminarity (LAM), trapping time (TT), entropy (ENTR), longest diagonal line (Lmax)
Step 5: Test group differences in each CRQA metric across severity groups
Step 6: Fit partial correlation models: CRQA_DET ~ frailty_index, adjusting for age/site/HbA1c/BMI/broadband_coupling
Step 7: Negative control: compute CRQA on randomly paired participants (same site) and verify no group signal
Step 8: Test incremental predictive value of CRQA metrics beyond broadband coupling features
test_plan.expected_effect_size: Cohen's d 0.3-0.5 for DET and LAM across severity gradient
test_plan.success_criterion: CRQA DET and LAM increase with diabetes severity (FDR p < 0.01) and predict frailty beyond broadband coupling
test_plan.refutation_criterion: No group differences in any CRQA metric. CRQA metrics are fully redundant with broadband Pearson r (no incremental value). Negative control (random pairing) shows similar group differences.
sensitivity_checks: Vary recurrence threshold to achieve 2%, 5%, 10% recurrence rate
Compare fixed E=3 vs data-driven E selection
Segment into 24h blocks and average CRQA metrics to assess stationarity
Test windowed CRQA (12h windows) for temporal variation of CRQA metrics
Compare with MdCRQA (multidimensional CRQA including activity as third variable)
secondary_methods: Joint recurrence plots (including activity as third dimension)
Symbolic dynamics / permutation-based cross-recurrence

notes: Novel analytical angle on the coupling data. CRQA captures nonlinear dynamical properties (determinism, trapping) that correlation and entropy miss. High computational cost and less familiar to clinical audiences.

title: Glucose-HR coupling strength has a U-shaped relationship with sleep quality
statement: Within each diabetes severity group, glucose-HR coupling shows a U-shaped (quadratic) relationship with sleep quality metrics (sleep efficiency, total sleep time): both very poor and very good sleepers have stronger glucose-HR coupling than moderate sleepers. Poor sleep increases coupling through sleep fragmentation-driven sympathetic activation. Paradoxically, very deep/efficient sleep also shows stronger coupling because autonomic regulation during consolidated deep sleep creates coherent glucose-HR co-modulation through intact parasympathetic control of hepatic glucose output. The quadratic term is strongest in the pre-diabetes and oral medication groups, where autonomic function is partially but not fully impaired.
mechanism: Sleep quality modulates autonomic balance bidirectionally. Poor sleep (low efficiency, high WASO, fragmented) increases sympathetic activation and reduces vagal tone, which amplifies the pathological glucose-HR locking by removing autonomic buffering. High-quality deep sleep, conversely, involves strong parasympathetic drive that coherently modulates both hepatic glucose output (via vagal regulation of liver) and HR (via vagal bradycardia), creating a different form of glucose-HR co-regulation. At moderate sleep quality, neither mechanism dominates, producing the weakest coupling. In early/moderate diabetes (pre-diabetes, oral medication), autonomic function is partially impaired: enough to create the sympathetic arm of the U-shape (poor sleep drives coupling up) but with enough residual vagal function to create the parasympathetic arm (deep sleep also drives coupling up). In advanced diabetes, rigid sympathetic dominance flattens the U-shape because coupling is high regardless of sleep quality.
predictions: Within each diabetes severity group, a quadratic model (coupling ~ sleep_efficiency + sleep_efficiency^2) fits significantly better than linear (p < 0.01 for quadratic term) for at least the pre-diabetes and oral medication groups
The U-shape minimum (weakest coupling) occurs at moderate sleep efficiency (75-85%)
In healthy participants, the U-shape is attenuated (flatter) because autonomic regulation buffers sleep quality effects
In insulin-dependent participants, the U-shape is attenuated because coupling is rigidly high regardless of sleep quality
Negative control: glucose-activity coupling does NOT show a U-shaped relationship with sleep quality (activity coupling is behaviorally driven, not autonomically)

literature.title: Slow-oscillation/spindle coupling predicts next-day fasting glucose
literature.key_finding: Sleep quality (specifically SO-spindle coupling) modulates next-day glucose; autonomic activity during sleep mediates the effect.
literature.relevance: Establishes that sleep quality modulates glucose-autonomic dynamics; we test whether this manifests as a nonlinear coupling-sleep relationship.

literature.title: Mining associations between glycemic variability in awake-time and in-sleep among non-diabetic adults
literature.key_finding: In-sleep glycemic variability is associated with awake-time glycemic variability and sleep quality metrics from wearables.
literature.relevance: Shows that sleep quality metrics from consumer wearables relate to glucose dynamics, supporting the feasibility of this analysis.

feasibility.statistical_power: N~1500 with sleep data x ~8 nights = ~12,000 night-coupling pairs
key_challenges: Garmin sleep staging is consumer-grade; sleep efficiency estimates are approximate
U-shaped relationships need sufficient range in sleep quality (restricted range reduces power)
Must use mixed-effects models to handle repeated measures within person
dataset_limitations: Consumer-grade sleep staging may misclassify sleep architecture
10 nights per person limits the range of sleep quality variation
No PSG validation of Garmin sleep metrics

test_plan.primary_method: Mixed-effects polynomial regression: nocturnal_coupling ~ sleep_efficiency + sleep_efficiency^2 + (1|person_id), stratified by study group
implementation_steps: Step 1: Compute per-night glucose-HR coupling (Pearson r during Garmin-detected sleep)
Step 2: Extract per-night sleep efficiency, total sleep time, WASO from Garmin sleep data
Step 3: Fit mixed-effects model with linear + quadratic sleep efficiency terms per study group
Step 4: Compare quadratic vs linear model fit using AIC/BIC and likelihood ratio test
Step 5: Identify the sleep efficiency value at the coupling minimum (vertex of quadratic)
Step 6: Test group interaction: does the curvature (quadratic coefficient) differ by diabetes severity?
Step 7: Negative control: same analysis with glucose-activity coupling instead of glucose-HR
Step 8: Replicate with total sleep time and with WASO as alternative sleep quality metrics
test_plan.expected_effect_size: Quadratic coefficient significantly different from zero; U-shape curvature d 0.15-0.25 across middle severity groups
test_plan.success_criterion: Significant quadratic term (p < 0.01) in at least pre-diabetes and oral medication groups, with U-shape minimum at moderate sleep efficiency
test_plan.refutation_criterion: Linear model fits as well or better than quadratic in all groups. No U-shape: coupling monotonically decreases or increases with sleep quality. Glucose-activity coupling shows the same pattern (non-specific).
sensitivity_checks: Use cubic spline instead of quadratic to test for more complex nonlinearity
Stratify by weekday vs weekend nights
Exclude very short nights (<4h total sleep time)
Use deep sleep percentage instead of sleep efficiency
Bootstrap 1000x to assess stability of the quadratic coefficient
secondary_methods: GAM (generalized additive model) for flexible nonlinear fitting
Quantile regression to test U-shape at different coupling quantiles

notes: Risky hypothesis: the U-shaped prediction is specific and could easily be refuted. But if confirmed, it reveals a nuanced coupling-sleep interaction that could inform sleep-targeted diabetes interventions. Garmin sleep quality is the main measurement concern.

title: Frailty is better predicted by coupling feature instability than by coupling feature level
statement: Frailty index (the strongest clinical discriminator of diabetes severity in AI-READI, AUROC 0.90) is better predicted by the instability (variance, range, entropy) of coupling features across the 10-day window than by their mean levels. This is because frailty reflects cumulative regulatory failure (deficit accumulation), and the instability of coupling captures moment-to-moment regulatory strain, whereas mean coupling reflects a chronic steady-state adaptation.
mechanism: Frailty in the Rockwood deficit-accumulation framework is the fraction of bodily systems that have crossed their failure threshold. Each failed system reduces the organism's ability to maintain stable inter-organ coordination under varying daily demands. This manifests not as a fixed coupling pattern but as erratic, unpredictable coupling: some hours show pathologically high coupling (sympathetic storms), others show decoupled dynamics (autonomic fatigue), and the transitions between these states are less organized. The variance and range of coupling features across the 10-day window capture this regulatory instability. Mean coupling, by contrast, reflects the average state, which may converge to a deceptively 'normal' value even in frail individuals whose coupling oscillates wildly.
predictions: Variance of glucose-HR coupling features (computed across days or 4h blocks within each person's 10-day window) predicts frailty index better than mean coupling (incremental R2 > 0.03)
Range (max - min) of daily coupling also predicts frailty independently
The instability-frailty association survives adjustment for age, site, HbA1c, BMI, and mean coupling level
Negative control: instability of glucose MEAN across days does not predict frailty as well (coupling instability is specific, not just glycemic instability)
Instability features also improve allostatic load prediction but less strongly than frailty prediction

literature.title: Disruption of multisystem responses to stress in type 2 diabetes
literature.key_finding: Multisystem response instability (erratic stress reactivity and recovery) characterizes T2D, consistent with allostatic load model.
literature.relevance: Supports the idea that instability of physiological responses (not just their mean level) reflects disease burden.

literature.title: A Study of Physical Resilience and Aging (SPRING): Conceptual Framework
literature.journal: Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
literature.key_finding: Resilience in aging is the ability to maintain homeostasis under perturbation; reduced resilience manifests as increased variability in physiological responses.
literature.relevance: Theoretical framework connecting response instability to frailty and reduced resilience.

feasibility.time_resolution_needed: per-day or per-4h-block (then summarize instability per person)
feasibility.statistical_power: N~1900; well-powered for R2 comparison between mean and variance features
key_challenges: With only 10 days, variance estimates are noisy (df ~ 8-9 for daily estimates)
Instability may correlate strongly with mean level (collinearity)
Must separate measurement noise from genuine physiological instability
dataset_limitations: 10-day window limits variance estimation precision
Cross-sectional: cannot determine whether instability precedes or follows frailty
No longitudinal outcomes to validate instability as a prognostic marker

test_plan.primary_method: Compare predictive models: frailty ~ mean_coupling_features vs frailty ~ instability_features (variance, range, entropy of coupling across days/blocks) vs combined model
implementation_steps: Step 1: For each participant, segment 10-day window into overlapping 4h blocks (stride=2h)
Step 2: Compute glucose-HR coupling (Pearson r, Spearman r) within each 4h block
Step 3: Compute per-person: mean, SD, CV, range, IQR, Shannon entropy (binned) of block-level coupling values
Step 4: Fit Ridge regression: frailty ~ mean_coupling_features + age + site + HbA1c + BMI (Model A)
Step 5: Fit Ridge regression: frailty ~ instability_features + age + site + HbA1c + BMI (Model B)
Step 6: Fit combined: frailty ~ mean_features + instability_features + covariates (Model C)
Step 7: Compare R2 of Model A, B, C on held-out test set
Step 8: Negative control: same with glucose mean instability instead of coupling instability
test_plan.expected_effect_size: Incremental R2 > 0.03 from instability features beyond mean features for frailty prediction
test_plan.success_criterion: Model B (instability only) outperforms Model A (mean only) for frailty prediction, and Model C (combined) outperforms both
test_plan.refutation_criterion: Model A outperforms Model B. Instability features are fully redundant with mean features (Model C no better than Model A). Glucose mean instability predicts frailty equally well.
sensitivity_checks: Use 6h and 12h blocks instead of 4h
Use per-day coupling instead of per-block
Robust variance estimation (MAD, IQR) instead of SD
Cross-validate with train/val/test split
Test for confounding: does instability correlate with data completeness?
secondary_methods: Functional data analysis: coupling as a function of time, predict frailty from shape features
Random forest feature importance for mean vs instability features

notes: Complementary to H-NEW11 (day-to-day CV) but more focused on frailty prediction and using finer temporal resolution (4h blocks). The practical implication: if instability predicts frailty better, monitoring coupling VARIABILITY over time becomes more clinically useful than a single coupling measurement.

title: Glucose-HR coupling strength exhibits a circadian rhythm that flattens with diabetes severity
statement: In healthy individuals, glucose-HR coupling strength follows a diurnal pattern: weaker coupling during the morning (when circadian cortisol peak drives glucose independently of HR), peak coupling in the afternoon (when meal-driven glucose and activity-driven HR co-vary most), and intermediate coupling at night (sleep-mode coupling). In diabetes, this circadian modulation of coupling strength flattens: coupling is persistently elevated regardless of time of day, reflecting the loss of circadian modulation of autonomic responsiveness.
mechanism: Circadian rhythms modulate autonomic tone (vagal tone peaks at night; sympathetic tone peaks during the day), cortisol (morning peak drives hepatic glucose output independently), and behavioral patterns (meals, activity clustered in daytime). These circadian variations create time-of-day-dependent glucose-HR coupling: morning glucose is cortisol-driven (decoupled from HR), afternoon glucose is meal+activity-driven (coupled to HR through postprandial autonomic responses), and nighttime coupling reflects basal autonomic-metabolic coordination. In diabetes, the loss of autonomic circadian modulation (autonomic neuropathy flattens day-night HR variability) and the persistence of insulin resistance-driven glucose elevation throughout the day create a flat coupling profile: the system is locked into pathological glucose-HR co-elevation regardless of time of day.
predictions: In healthy individuals, time-of-day-specific glucose-HR coupling peaks in the afternoon (12-6pm local time) and is lowest in the morning (6-10am)
The amplitude of this diurnal coupling rhythm (peak - trough) is largest in healthy and decreases with diabetes severity (d > 0.3)
In insulin-dependent participants, glucose-HR coupling is relatively flat across the day (low diurnal amplitude)
The overall level of coupling is higher in diabetes at all times of day, but the TIME-OF-DAY VARIATION is reduced
Negative control: glucose-activity coupling should show preserved diurnal variation even in diabetes (activity is behaviorally driven, not autonomically)

literature.title: Circadian Regulation of Glucose, Lipid, and Energy Metabolism in Humans
literature.key_finding: Glucose tolerance, insulin sensitivity, and energy metabolism all exhibit circadian rhythms that are disrupted in metabolic disease.
literature.relevance: Establishes the circadian regulation of glucose metabolism that should create time-of-day-varying coupling.

literature.title: HRV in sleep stages is associated with metabolic function and glycemic control in T2D
literature.key_finding: Heart rate variability during different sleep stages differs between T2D patients and controls, with T2D showing reduced circadian HRV modulation.
literature.relevance: Supports the prediction that diabetes flattens the circadian modulation of autonomic function, which should flatten coupling diurnal patterns.

feasibility.statistical_power: N~1900 x 10 days = well-powered for time-of-day x group interaction
key_challenges: Time-of-day coupling estimates require sufficient points per block (~24-48 per 2h block per day)
Meal timing varies; the afternoon peak may shift with meal schedule
Timezone alignment is critical; must use local time
dataset_limitations: No meal timing: cannot separate meal-driven coupling from circadian-driven coupling
Garmin activity data confounds time-of-day coupling (afternoon coupling may be activity-driven)
Cross-site timezone differences need careful handling

test_plan.primary_method: Compute glucose-HR coupling in 4h time-of-day bins (pooled across days per person), fit cosinor model to diurnal coupling profile, extract amplitude and acrophase, test group differences
implementation_steps: Step 1: Bin all aligned glucose-HR data into 4h time-of-day blocks (6am-10am, 10am-2pm, 2pm-6pm, 6pm-10pm, 10pm-2am, 2am-6am, local time)
Step 2: Compute glucose-HR Pearson r within each 4h block per person (pooling across days)
Step 3: Fit cosinor model to the 6-point diurnal coupling profile per person
Step 4: Extract diurnal coupling amplitude and acrophase
Step 5: Test group differences in diurnal amplitude (expect decrease with severity)
Step 6: Test group differences in mean coupling level (expect increase with severity, from H-MIG01)
Step 7: Confirm that amplitude decreases faster than mean level increases (ratio analysis)
Step 8: Negative control: same analysis for glucose-activity coupling
test_plan.expected_effect_size: Cohen's d 0.3-0.5 for diurnal amplitude decrease across severity gradient
test_plan.success_criterion: Diurnal coupling amplitude decreases monotonically with diabetes severity (FDR p < 0.01), even after adjusting for mean coupling level
test_plan.refutation_criterion: Diurnal coupling amplitude does not differ across groups. Diabetes increases both mean and amplitude proportionally (no flattening). Glucose-activity coupling shows equal diurnal amplitude changes.
sensitivity_checks: Use 2h blocks instead of 4h for finer time-of-day resolution
Stratify by weekday vs weekend
Adjust for time-of-day activity level (partial correlation approach)
Test stability: first 5 days vs last 5 days
Compare awake-only blocks to full 24h blocks
secondary_methods: Random-effects cosinor model for simultaneous diurnal + group estimation
Functional ANOVA on diurnal coupling curves

notes: Suggested in the preliminary results doc as a next step (circadian stratification). This formalizes it as a testable hypothesis about diurnal AMPLITUDE of coupling, not just mean level.

title: HR complexity loss (multiscale entropy) amplifies the glucose-HR coupling signal in diabetes
statement: Participants with lower HR multiscale entropy (less complex HR dynamics, indicating more severe autonomic neuropathy) show stronger glucose-HR coupling than those with higher HR complexity, within each diabetes severity group. This interaction means that HR complexity moderates the coupling signal: the coupling increase in diabetes is partly driven by the loss of HR degrees of freedom (simplified HR dynamics become more 'capturable' by glucose variations). Formally, there is a negative interaction between HR MSE and diabetes severity in predicting glucose-HR coupling.
mechanism: In a complex HR time series (healthy autonomic regulation), many independent controllers modulate HR: baroreflexes, respiratory sinus arrhythmia, thermoregulatory vasomotion, and activity-driven changes. Glucose is only one of many inputs, so glucose-HR coupling is diluted by these other influences. When autonomic neuropathy reduces HR complexity (fewer active controllers), glucose becomes a proportionally larger driver of HR variation, increasing the apparent coupling. This is analogous to signal-to-noise improvement: when the 'noise' of complex autonomous HR dynamics is reduced, the 'signal' of glucose-driven HR changes becomes more visible. This mechanism predicts that within a diabetes severity group, those with lower HR complexity show stronger coupling.
predictions: HR MSE (at scales 3-12) is negatively correlated with glucose-HR coupling (r < -0.15) after adjusting for study group, age, and HbA1c
There is a significant HR_MSE x study_group_ordinal interaction on coupling: the coupling increase with severity is amplified in participants with lower HR MSE
Glucose MSE does not show the same moderating effect (the mechanism is specific to HR complexity, not glucose complexity)
Controlling for HR MSE attenuates (but does not eliminate) the coupling-severity gradient, indicating partial mediation
Negative control: HR MSE does not moderate glucose-activity coupling as strongly (activity coupling is behaviorally driven)

literature.title: Heart rate variability and complexity in people with diabetes associated cardiac autonomic neuropathy
literature.key_finding: Both HRV and HR complexity are reduced in diabetic cardiac autonomic neuropathy, with multiscale entropy showing greater diagnostic sensitivity than traditional HRV metrics.
literature.relevance: Establishes that HR MSE is reduced in diabetic autonomic neuropathy, providing the basis for our interaction hypothesis.

literature.title: Loss of 'complexity' and aging: potential applications of fractals and chaos theory to senescence
literature.key_finding: Disease and aging reduce physiological complexity; this loss of complexity reduces the system's ability to adapt to perturbations.
literature.relevance: Theoretical framework for why complexity loss in HR dynamics would amplify the apparent coupling with glucose.

literature.title: Permutation entropy analysis of heart rate variability for the assessment of cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy in type 1 diabetes mellitus
literature.key_finding: Permutation entropy of HR detects CAN earlier than traditional HRV metrics, supporting entropy-based measures of autonomic function.
literature.relevance: Validates entropy measures of HR as clinically relevant autonomic neuropathy markers.

feasibility.analysis_timescale: per-person summary (MSE from 10-day HR, coupling from 10-day glucose-HR)
feasibility.statistical_power: N~1900; sufficient for interaction terms with medium effect sizes
key_challenges: HR MSE from 5-min averaged Garmin data may not capture the fine-grained complexity that beat-to-beat HR would
Collinearity between HR MSE, mean HR, and coupling features
Formal SampEn computation for HR at multiple scales (not the existing Shannon proxy)
dataset_limitations: Garmin HR is smoothed/averaged; true HR complexity (beat-to-beat) is not available

Medications affecting HR dynamics are redacted

test_plan.primary_method: Moderation analysis: coupling ~ study_group * HR_MSE + covariates, testing whether HR complexity moderates the coupling-severity relationship
implementation_steps: Step 1: Compute formal HR SampEn at scales 1,3,6,12,24 from 10-day 5-min HR time series per participant
Step 2: Compute HR complexity index (CI_HR) as area under MSE curve for scales 3-12
Step 3: Compute per-person glucose-HR coupling features (from existing coupling_features.parquet)
Step 4: Fit moderation model: glucose_hr_awake_r ~ study_group_ordinal * CI_HR + age + site + HbA1c + BMI
Step 5: Test significance of the interaction term
Step 6: Test mediation: does adjusting for CI_HR attenuate the coupling-severity gradient?
Step 7: Negative control: repeat with glucose MSE as moderator (should be weaker)
Step 8: Compare existing Shannon entropy proxy vs formal SampEn for HR
test_plan.expected_effect_size: Interaction beta such that a 1-SD decrease in HR MSE corresponds to a 0.02-0.04 increase in coupling, beyond severity main effect
test_plan.success_criterion: Significant negative HR_MSE x severity interaction on coupling (p < 0.01), with partial mediation of the coupling-severity gradient by HR MSE
test_plan.refutation_criterion: No interaction between HR MSE and severity on coupling. HR MSE is fully redundant with HR mean or HR SD. Glucose MSE shows the same moderating effect (non-specific).
sensitivity_checks: Compare Shannon entropy proxy vs formal SampEn
Stratify by awake/sleep to test if moderation differs by state
Control for mean HR level (HR MSE may correlate with mean HR)
Test with the 11-second ECG RMSSD as an alternative autonomic measure
Bootstrap the interaction term 1000x
secondary_methods: Structural equation model: severity -> HR_MSE -> coupling (path analysis)
Conditional random forest: importance of HR_MSE for coupling prediction

notes: This addresses WHY coupling increases in diabetes: partly because HR dynamics become simpler, making glucose a relatively larger HR driver. Important mechanistic refinement. Garmin HR quality is the main concern.
